humanities_role_explanation: Historical newspaper text (19th-century British crime news) supplies the items, but the competence tested is generic post-OCR error correction (sequence-to-sequence / instruction-following), measured by CER reduction; no disciplinary interpretive competence is assessed.
benchmark_modalities_explanation: Text only: OCR output strings are paired with manually re-keyed ground-truth transcriptions; page images are not given to models.
analytical_tasks_explanation: Post-OCR correction: models map erroneous OCR text to the accurate reference ('Fix the OCR errors in the provided text'), including substitutions, insertions, deletions, misnamed entities and hallucinated text. Framed as neural machine translation for BART and as prompt-based instruction-tuning for Llama 2.

general_purpose_benchmark.note: Scoped to a single task (post-OCR correction) on a single corpus, BLN600.

evaluates_generative_llm.note: Instruction-tuned (LoRA) Llama 2 7B and 13B base models, compared against fine-tuned BART (encoder-decoder, not generative LLM).

quantitative_metrics.note: Percentage reduction in character error rate (CER), mean over five runs.

summary: The paper instruction-tunes Llama 2 (7B, 13B) with LoRA for post-OCR correction of BLN600, a parallel corpus of 19th-century British newspaper articles, and compares it with fine-tuned BART. Llama 2 13B reduces CER by 54.51% versus 23.30% for BART large, and Llama 2 performs well even with little training data.
key_findings: Llama 2 13B achieves 54.51% CER reduction, Llama 2 7B 43.26%, BART large 23.30%, BART base 14.60%. Llama 2 is strong with only 80 training samples while BART improves substantially with more data. Substitutions and deletions are easiest to correct; insertions and misnamed entities are harder, and hallucinated OCR text is mostly uncorrectable.
evaluation_unit: sequence pair (OCR segment and ground-truth segment, mostly sentences)
gold_upstream: BLN600 (Booth et al., 2024): OCR text from British Library Newspapers paired with manually re-keyed human transcriptions from the source images; further production details not described in this paper.
facets_explanation: Reference texts are the manually re-keyed human transcriptions of BLN600, an existing corpus by overlapping authors (Booth et al., 2024). The paper does not describe who re-keyed them or how disagreement was handled. The correct output is determined by the OCR input's source text and scored against one reference via CER.
results_explanation: Table 3 lists 'Llama 2 13B 54.51' as CER Reduction (%), the best result, versus 'BART 400M 23.30'. The values are means over five training and evaluation iterations. The metric is percentage CER reduction rather than raw CER, hence 'other'. The training-size comparison (Fig. 3) varies training data, an ablation, so it is not counted as a format gap. No human baseline is reported.

humanities_role.quote: Poor OCR quality continues to be a major obstacle for humanities scholars seeking to make use of digitised primary sources such as historical newspapers.

primary_evaluation_setting.quote: By instruction-tuning Llama 2 and comparing it to a fine-tuned BART on BLN600

gold_source.quote: This dataset contains OCR text sourced from British Library Newspapers along with manually re-keyed human transcriptions.

gold_beyond_stimulus.quote: Correction of misnamed entities including names, locations and organisations is of particular interest to improve text mining results.

answer_multiplicity.quote: computing the Levenshtein distance between the recognised text and the reference text
